newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Netanyahu refuses to rule out Golan pullout.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu refuses to rule out Golan pullout.

text.p: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu sparked speculation in the Jewish state on Monday by declining to rule out a future land-for-peace swap with Syria on the Israeli-held Golan Heights.

Shortly after he defeated Shimon Peres in a closely-fought May election, Netanyahu alarmed Arabs by rejecting the formula of trading occupied territory for peace, the American-endorsed cornerstone of Israeli foreign policy under Peres's Labour.

But in interviews with Israeli reporters en route to Washington for talks with President Bill Clinton on Monday, Netanyahu repeatedly refrained from answering directly when asked if he would rule out territorial compromise on the Golan.

"If Syria truly desires negotiations, we can certainly find the required formula (to restart them), with the help also of the United States and President Clinton," Netanyahu told Israel's Channel Two television.

Pressed for an outright rejection of returning Golan territory, Netanyahu told the television "Listen, I believe that the main problem at the moment is how to overcome the Syrian demand that we give up the Golan Heights as a condition to opening talks on the Golan Heights."
Five years of sporadic Israeli-Syrian talks have foundered over the Golan, captured by Israel in the 1967 Middle East war.

Damascus demands Israel return all the lands it holds on the strategic plateau. Peres and his slain predecessor Yitzhak Rabin expressed willingness for at least a partial Golan withdrawal, a stance Netanyahu has blasted as compromising Israel's security.

"Is Netanyahu changing his position on substantive issues?" Channel Two political correspondent Emmanuel Rozen asked rhetorically in a report on the Netanyahu-Clinton meeting, expected to focus on ways to resuscitate the Syria talks and smooth rough-and-tumble negotiations with the Palestinians.

Analysts have paid close attention to the nuances of media-master Netanyahu's public statements, particularly since a progressive softening of the prime minister's declarations on the possibility of a summit with PLO leader Yasser Arafat was capped last week by a breakthough meeting between the two once-arch foes.

In a separate interview with Israel's Channel One television Netanyahu said on Monday rejection of trading Golan land remained "the basic position of this government, and I see no reason to give up on it as the price for entering the talks.
"We will also aspire to end the talks with exactly that position."
